sections.heading: Recognizing that everything I have comes from you
sections.text: Great I AM, everything I have is from you. My life, my breath, every good thing I enjoy, every step forward, every ordinary ability to see, hear, touch, think, love, and receive beauty—all of it is your gift. Nothing that makes life good or meaningful comes from me first. I receive it from your hand.
theological_themes: God is the source and giver of life and every good gift.
Human life is dependent on God not only for spiritual blessings but for ordinary created gifts.
Thanksgiving begins by acknowledging that nothing good is self-produced.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells the Athenians that God gives life, breath, and everything, and that all people live and move in him. This directly supports the prayer’s confession that even ordinary existence and ability are received from God.
James grounds every good gift in the unchanging generosity of God. This helps frame happiness, beauty, truth, and daily provision as gifts rather than possessions earned or owned independently.

sections.heading: Owning my need for your grace
sections.text: And in my life with you, I am just as dependent—completely dependent. Please give me the grace to see how much I need grace. Show me my sin honestly, so I will not hide it or defend it. Show me my weakness, so I will stop pretending I am strong on my own and learn to find my strength in you.
theological_themes: Grace is needed even to recognize the need for grace.
True self-knowledge before God includes both sin and weakness.
God’s strength is known most deeply by those who stop relying on themselves.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This grounds the prayer’s confession of total spiritual dependence rather than self-sufficiency.
Paul learns that Christ’s power is made perfect in weakness. This supports the request to understand personal weakness not as the end of hope, but as the place where God’s strength is known.

sections.heading: Confessing the sin I would rather excuse
sections.text: Thank you for any real sorrow over sin that is already in me. Please deepen it. My sin is not light or harmless; it runs deeper than I like to admit. It comes from a heart that can be hard, proud, and quick to justify itself. Help me confess without making excuses, without presenting myself as better than I am, and without pretending I have earned anything from you. Let my repentance be honest, grieving, and humble before you.
theological_themes: Sin is serious and rooted in the heart, not merely in outward actions.
Repentance is itself a gift from God and should be desired more deeply.
Confession rejects self-justification and comes to God without claims of merit.

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession shows sin as first and finally an offense before God, not something to minimize or excuse. It gives biblical shape to honest repentance that appeals to mercy rather than merit.
This passage shows that God receives a broken and contrite heart rather than religious performance used as a cover. It supports the prayer’s desire for genuine sorrow instead of self-defense.
John warns against denying sin and holds out God’s faithful forgiveness to those who confess. This supports both the honesty of confession and the hope that confession is not hopeless despair.

sections.heading: Asking you to heal what is sick in me
sections.text: I need healing, not just improvement. Good Physician, there is more than enough in me for you to work on. Come near and show your power where I am diseased by sin, pride, unbelief, and self-reliance. Do in me what I cannot do for myself.
theological_themes: Sin is not only guilt but spiritual sickness needing divine healing.
God’s saving power reaches people who cannot cure themselves.
The image of God as physician expresses both mercy and authority.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies himself as the physician who comes for sinners rather than the self-righteous. This directly grounds the prayer’s appeal for healing from the one who came to call and restore the spiritually sick.
Jeremiah asks the Lord for healing and salvation together, recognizing that restoration must come from God. This supports the prayer’s cry for God to heal what the worshiper cannot repair.

sections.heading: Strengthening the faith you have given me
sections.text: I need faith, and even that has come from you. Please keep it alive, make it stronger, and grow it deeper. Fix my trust on the finished work of the Savior, on the greatness and fatherly majesty of the Father, and on the living work of the Spirit in me. Work in me now, so that I do not treat you as doubtful or unreliable, but trust you as the true, powerful, and faithful God you are.
theological_themes: Faith is a gift from God and must be sustained by God.
Christian faith is centered on Christ’s saving work and lived before the triune God.
Trust grows as God reveals himself as truthful, mighty, and faithful.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that salvation by grace through faith is God’s gift, not a ground for boasting. This supports the prayer’s request that God maintain and increase the very faith he has given.
Believers are called to look to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith. This grounds the prayer’s desire to have faith centered on the Savior’s work rather than on the believer’s own stability.

Peter frames Christian life in relation to the Father’s foreknowledge, the Spirit’s sanctifying work, and obedience to Jesus Christ. This supports the prayer’s explicitly Trinitarian orientation without forcing a later formula onto the text.

sections.heading: Bringing back to you the fruit you grow in me
sections.text: Then I can come to you with a heart full of love, gratitude, hope, and joy. And even those are not my achievements; they are fruit from your own garden. Let me lay them at your feet. Teach me to love you with a love that does not grow cold, to trust you with a confidence that does not collapse, to hope in you with expectation that does not fade, and to delight in you with joy that cannot be smothered. Use the best of me to honor you. Let my life catch and reflect something of your own glory.
theological_themes: Love, gratitude, hope, and joy are fruits of God’s work in the believer, not grounds for boasting.
The proper end of spiritual growth is worship and the glorifying of God.
Believers reflect God’s glory as they are transformed by him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes love, joy, and related virtues as the fruit of the Spirit rather than self-generated moral achievement. This supports the image of bringing God the fruit that he himself has grown.

Jesus connects abiding in him with bearing fruit, glorifying the Father, remaining in his love, and receiving his joy. This passage closely supports the prayer’s movement from dependence to fruitfulness, love, joy, and God’s glory.
Paul describes believers being transformed as they behold the Lord’s glory. This grounds the prayer’s desire to reflect God’s glory rather than merely perform religious devotion.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses intense penitential language such as sins being 'black and deep' and asks for confession with 'self-loathing.' I preserved the seriousness of sin and the rejection of self-justification while avoiding language that could be heard as hatred of creaturely personhood rather than hatred of sin.

The prayer addresses God as 'Great I AM' and later 'Good Physician.' In Christian use, the physician image is strongly associated with Christ, while the prayer remains addressed to God. The adaptation keeps the address broad enough to preserve the original devotional flow while the Scripture references include Jesus’ own physician imagery.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'know my strength in thee' through the biblical pattern of divine strength being known in human weakness, rather than as a request for self-confidence.

I rendered 'fruits grown in thy garden' as love, gratitude, hope, and joy produced by God and returned to him, preserving the original’s insistence that even the worshiper’s best responses are gifts of grace.

I kept the Trinitarian movement—Savior’s work, Father’s majesty, Spirit’s operations—without expanding it into a systematic explanation, since the original names these as the proper center and support of faith rather than as a separate doctrinal meditation.
